summary.text: Grouping subsets by their size and applying a root-of-unity filter, together with factoring the generating product into complete root-of-unity blocks, shows that the count differs from \(M_n=\sum_{k=1}^n \binom nk/k\) by only \(O(n2^{n/2})\). The identity \(M_n=\sum_{j=1}^n(2^j-1)/j\) is then reflected about \(j=n\) and \(1/(n-i)\) expanded through degree five; the geometric moments \(\sum_{i\ge0} i^t/2^i\) give the stated coefficients, while geometric tail bounds make both remainders negligible at the required scale.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\left\{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:\frac1{|S|}\sum_{x\in S}x\in\mathbb Z\right\}.
\]
For \(1\le k\le n\), write
\[
N(n,k)=\#\left\{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:|S|=k,\quad k\mid\sum_{x\in S}x\right\}.
\]
Every nonempty subset has a unique cardinality \(k\), and its average is an integer exactly when its sum is divisible by \(k\). Hence
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n N(n,k). \tag{1}
\]

We first show that, uniformly in \(1\le k\le n\),
\[
\left|N(n,k)-\frac1k\binom nk\right|\le 2^{(n+1)/2}, \tag{2}
\]
where, when the exponent is written in this form in an inequality involving integer powers, it means \(2^{\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor}\). This is the combinatorial estimate that makes all nontrivial congruence classes negligible.

Fix \(k\), and let \(\zeta=e^{2\pi i/k}\), a primitive \(k\)-th root of unity. For \(0\le j<k\), define
\[
f_j=[X^k]\prod_{r=1}^n(1+\zeta^{jr}X).
\]
Expanding the product gives
\[
f_j=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\ |S|=k}}
 \zeta^{j\sum_{r\in S}r}. \tag{3}
\]
The elementary roots-of-unity filter says that for every integer \(s\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\zeta^{js}=
\begin{cases}
k,&k\mid s,\\0,&k\nmid s.
\end{cases} \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, in the first case every term is 1, and otherwise this is a geometric sum with ratio different from 1 and with ratio's \(k\)-th power equal to 1. Summing (3) over \(j\) and applying (4) therefore gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}f_j=kN(n,k). \tag{5}
\]
Also \(f_0=[X^k](1+X)^n=\binom nk\). Consequently
\[
N(n,k)-\frac1k\binom nk=\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}f_j. \tag{6}
\]

It remains to bound the nontrivial coefficients \(f_j\). For a complex polynomial \(P(X)=\sum c_rX^r\), put
\[
\|P\|_1=\sum_r|c_r|.
\]
The triangle inequality for convolution gives
\[
\|PQ\|_1\le \|P\|_1\|Q\|_1,
\]
and every coefficient satisfies \(|[X^r]P|\le\|P\|_1\).

Let \(w=\zeta^j\) for some \(1\le j<k\), and let \(m\) be its multiplicative order. Then \(m\mid k\). Since \(w\ne1\), we have \(m\ge2\), and since \(k\le n\), also \(m\le n\). The roots \(1,w,\ldots,w^{m-1}\) are all the \(m\)-th roots of unity. Thus, for every offset \(a\),
\[
\prod_{r=0}^{m-1}(1+w^{a+r}X)=1-(-X)^m. \tag{7}
\]
For example, (7) follows from \(\prod_{r=0}^{m-1}(1-w^rt)=1-t^m\), after taking \(t=-w^aX\) and using \((w^a)^m=1\).

Write \(n=mq+s\), where \(q=\lfloor n/m\rfloor\) and \(0\le s<m\). Splitting the product into \(q\) complete blocks of length \(m\) and one block of length \(s\), (7) gives
\[
\prod_{r=1}^n(1+w^rX)
=(1-(-X)^m)^q\prod_{r=1}^s(1+w^{mq+r}X).
\]
Now
\[
\|1-(-X)^m\|_1=2,
\qquad
\|1+w^rX\|_1=1+|w^r|=2.
\]
It follows by submultiplicativity that
\[
\left\|\prod_{r=1}^n(1+w^rX)\right\|_1\le 2^{q+s}. \tag{8}
\]
Moreover,
\[
q+s\le \left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\right\rfloor. \tag{9}
\]
To see this without any asymptotics, note that \(q\ge1\), \(s\le m-1\), and
\[
2(q+s)\le mq+s+1=n+1
\]
is equivalent to \((m-2)q\ge s-1\), which follows from
\((m-2)q\ge m-2\ge s-1\). Thus (8), (9), and the coefficient bound imply
\[
|f_j|\le 2^{\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor}.
\]
Applying this in (6) gives
\[
\left|N(n,k)-\frac1k\binom nk\right|
\le \frac{k-1}{k}\,2^{\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor}
\le 2^{\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor},
\]
which proves (2).

Define the main term and error by
\[
M(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k\binom nk,
\qquad E(n)=a(n)-M(n).
\]
By (1), (2), and the triangle inequality,
\[
|E(n)|
\le\sum_{k=1}^n\left|N(n,k)-\frac1k\binom nk\right|
\le n\,2^{\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor}. \tag{10}
\]
In particular,
\[
\frac{n^6E(n)}{2^{n+1}}\longrightarrow0. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, if \(A_n=2^{\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor}\), then \(A_n^2\le2^{n+1}\), so (10) yields
\[
\left|\frac{n^6E(n)}{2^{n+1}}\right|
\le \frac{n^7A_n}{2^{n+1}}\le\frac{n^7}{A_n}.
\]
Also \((\sqrt2)^n\le A_n\), since
\(n/2\le\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor\). Hence the last expression is at most
\(n^7/(\sqrt2)^n\), which tends to zero because an exponential with base greater than 1 dominates every fixed power.

We next analyze \(M(n)\). Pascal's identity gives the useful recurrence
\[
M(m+1)=M(m)+\frac{2^{m+1}-1}{m+1}. \tag{12}
\]
Here is the calculation. For \(1\le k\le m\),
\[
\binom{m+1}{k}=\binom m{k-1}+\binom mk,
\]
and the absorption identity gives
\[
\frac1k\binom m{k-1}=\frac1{m+1}\binom{m+1}{k}.
\]
Therefore the terms with \(1\le k\le m\) contribute
\[
M(m)+\frac1{m+1}\sum_{k=1}^m\binom{m+1}{k}
=M(m)+\frac{2^{m+1}-2}{m+1}.
\]
The remaining term \(k=m+1\) is \(1/(m+1)\), proving (12). Since \(M(0)=0\), summing the recurrence yields the exact identity
\[
M(n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{2^j-1}{j}=T(n)-H(n), \tag{13}
\]
where
\[
T(n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{2^j}{j},
\qquad H(n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j.
\]
The harmonic part is negligible on our scale. Since \(0\le H(n)\le n\),
\[
0\le\frac{n^6H(n)}{2^{n+1}}
\le\frac{n^7}{2^{n+1}}\longrightarrow0. \tag{14}
\]

We now derive a six-term expansion for \(T(n)\). Reflect its summation index by writing \(i=n-j\). Then
\[
\frac{n^6T(n)}{2^{n+1}}
=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{n^6}{(n-i)2^{i+1}}. \tag{15}
\]
For \(0\le i<n\), finite geometric division gives
\[
\frac{n^6}{n-i}
=\sum_{t=0}^5n^{5-t}i^t+\frac{i^6}{n-i}. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed,
\[
(n-i)\sum_{t=0}^5n^{5-t}i^t+i^6=n^6.
\]
Substituting (16) into (15), define
\[
S_t(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^t2^{-i},
\qquad
R(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2^{-(i+1)}\frac{i^6}{n-i}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{n^6T(n)}{2^{n+1}}
=\frac12\sum_{t=0}^5n^{5-t}S_t(n)+R(n). \tag{17}
\]

Let
\[
Q_t=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}i^t2^{-i}.
\]
These series converge, as does every polynomial times a geometric sequence of ratio \(1/2\). We need \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_5\). First \(Q_0=2\). For \(t\ge1\), shifting the summation index and using the binomial theorem gives
\[
Q_t=\frac12\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}(i+1)^t2^{-i}
=\frac12\sum_{r=0}^t\binom trQ_r.
\]
Thus
\[
2Q_t=\sum_{r=0}^t\binom trQ_r,
\qquad	ext{or equivalently}\qquad
Q_t=\sum_{r=0}^{t-1}\binom trQ_r. \tag{18}
\]
Successive use of (18) gives
\[
Q_0=2,
\quad Q_1=2,
\quad Q_2=6,
\quad Q_3=26,
\quad Q_4=150,
\quad Q_5=1082. \tag{19}
\]
For completeness, these are obtained as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_1&=Q_0=2,\\
Q_2&=Q_0+2Q_1=6,\\
Q_3&=Q_0+3Q_1+3Q_2=26,\\
Q_4&=Q_0+4Q_1+6Q_2+4Q_3=150,\\
Q_5&=Q_0+5Q_1+10Q_2+10Q_3+5Q_4=1082.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently
\[
\frac12\sum_{t=0}^5Q_tn^{5-t}
=n^5+n^4+3n^3+13n^2+75n+541. \tag{20}
\]
Denote the polynomial on the right by \(P(n)\).

We must justify replacing each truncated moment \(S_t(n)\) by \(Q_t\) in (17). For every \(0\le t\le5\),
\[
Q_t-S_t(n)=\sum_{i=n}^{\infty}i^t2^{-i}
=2^{-n}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}(n+r)^t2^{-r}.
\]
For \(n\ge1\),
\[
(n+r)^t\le(n+r)^5\le (n+1)^5(r+1)^5.
\]
Thus, with the finite constant
\[
K=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}(r+1)^5 2^{-r},
\]
we have
\[
0\le Q_t-S_t(n)\le K(n+1)^5 2^{-n}. \tag{21}
\]
Multiplying by \(n^5\), the right side still tends to zero, because it is bounded by a constant times \(n^{10}2^{-n}\). Therefore
\[
n^{5-t}\bigl(S_t(n)-Q_t\bigr)\longrightarrow0
\qquad(0\le t\le5), \tag{22}
\]
since for \(n\ge1\), \(n^{5-t}\le n^5\). Summing the six limits shows that the difference between the first term on the right of (17) and \(P(n)\) tends to zero.

It remains to prove
\[
R(n)\longrightarrow0. \tag{23}
\]
All terms of \(R(n)\) are nonnegative. Split the indices into the two ranges \(2i\le n\) and \(2i>n\).

If \(2i\le n\), then \(n-i\ge n/2\), and hence
\[
2^{-(i+1)}\frac{i^6}{n-i}
\le \frac2n\,2^{-(i+1)}i^6.
\]
Summing over this range, and then enlarging to all \(i\ge0\), gives
\[
\sum_{\substack{0\le i<n\\2i\le n}}
2^{-(i+1)}\frac{i^6}{n-i}
\le \frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}i^62^{-i}
=\frac{Q_6}{n}\longrightarrow0. \tag{24}
\]

If \(2i>n\), then \(i+1\ge\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor\), while \(i<n\), \(n-i\ge1\), and \(i^6\le n^6\). Therefore each term in this range is at most
\[
n^6 2^{-\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor}.
\]
There are fewer than \(n\) terms, so their total is at most
\[
\frac{n^7}{2^{\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor}}
\le\frac{n^7}{(\sqrt2)^n}\longrightarrow0. \tag{25}
\]
Together, (24) and (25) prove (23).

Combining (17), (20), (22), and (23), we obtain
\[
\frac{n^6T(n)}{2^{n+1}}-P(n)\longrightarrow0. \tag{26}
\]
Using \(M(n)=T(n)-H(n)\) from (13) and the negligible harmonic estimate (14), this becomes
\[
\frac{n^6M(n)}{2^{n+1}}-P(n)\longrightarrow0. \tag{27}
\]
Finally, \(a(n)=M(n)+E(n)\), and (11), (27) imply
\[
\frac{n^6a(n)}{2^{n+1}}-P(n)\longrightarrow0. \tag{28}
\]

For \(n\ge1\), factor \(P(n)\) as
\[
P(n)=n^5\left(1+\frac1n+\frac3{n^2}+\frac{13}{n^3}
+\frac{75}{n^4}+\frac{541}{n^5}\right). \tag{29}
\]
A direct rearrangement of (28), using (29), gives
\[
\frac{
 a(n)-\dfrac{2^{n+1}}n\left(1+\dfrac1n+\dfrac3{n^2}+\dfrac{13}{n^3}+\dfrac{75}{n^4}+\dfrac{541}{n^5}\right)
}{2^{n+1}/n^6}
\longrightarrow0. \tag{30}
\]
Thus the numerator in (30) is \(o(2^{n+1}/n^6)\). Since
\[
\frac{2^{n+1}}{n^6}=\frac{2^{n+1}}n\cdot\frac1{n^5},
\]
this is exactly
\[
a(n)=\frac{2^{n+1}}n\left(1+\frac1n+\frac3{n^2}+\frac{13}{n^3}+\frac{75}{n^4}+\frac{541}{n^5}+o\!\left(\frac1{n^5}\right)\right),
\]
as claimed.
